As I understand them:

Magic is basically technology, or method. A complex technique/method used to make something happen in an unconventional way. It earns the name "magic" if the method is mysterious/not known.

A miracle is something awesome (awe-inspiring, not the other meaning used in common parlance). It is more an event that is either great in magnitude or very improbable.

Magic is when you or someone else cause something to happen in a way that other people can't tell how it happened. A miracle is when something happens in a way that no one can tell how it happened.

Example: A man is pointing a gun at you and a group of friends. He says he's going to kill you all. You point at him and electricity flows out of your finger into the man with the gun. He is incapacitated. Magic.

A man is pointing a gun at you and a group of friends. He says he's going to kill you all. He suddenly gets struck by lightning. He is incapacitated. Miracle.

How do I even begin to Linux?

So people are going to reccomend many different distros (distributions, different flavours of Linux basically) and they really break down into two categories. Easy and hard. Which to go with iis really something you're going to have to decide for yourself.

Hard is the difficult to use distros like arch, gentoo, Slackware and so on. These distros will cause you a lot of pain initially to set up and will probably take a while for you to be comfortable in. This isn't necessarily a bad thing. The argument is that it will force you to become very knowledgeable in a comparatively short amount of time. I myself started with arch because of this. But you really need the drive to want to learn the ins and outs of Linux, if you don't then this will just frustrate you and push you back to windows.

On the other hand you have the more user friendly distros like mint and Ubuntu. These are actually far easier to use than you would think. Often the only difficulty people have with them is that it's not windows. But if you can get used to something that isn't windows I'd say most of these distros are actually easier to use than it. The problem with these distros is it gives you no incentive to learn much about Linux. This also isn't always a bad thing. After all, how much does the average window user really know about windows?

Anyways tl;Dr my advice would be to decide what kind of distro you want first and then work from there. There are plentyt of great offerings that won't let you down provided its the type for you. Good luck!

The question is a little vague. Please remember Linux is not Windows!

Also, IRC is a great resource to get on-the-fly tech help for your distro. Most distros have a channel on freeenode or another major IRC network, and should have instructions for connecting on their website.

Saving Files

Most Linux distros include the option to install alongside Windows, without wiping your Windows install. Linux (via ntfs-3g), supports Microsoft NTFS filesystems, such as most external hard drives, and you're base install of Windows. Most distros ship with ntfs-3g out of the box, so you should be able to access your files easily. Backing up to an external HDD should prove sufficient, two separate backups is always ideal (with any OS) though!

Code Proficiency

As others have mentioned, coding proficiency is not required. However, a basic understanding of the shell is helpful (but also not required). Google around for a guide. This one looks promising to me.

Task Manager

Most distros ship with a graphical process manager, usually called "system monitor". The specific software package will vary by distro, but "gnome-system-monitor" is the most common. There is also a robust selection of shell tools for process management as well. However, I doubt you will need to use anything like task manager during normal usage. Linux systems rarely hang, and most errors bad enough to cause the OS to hang will bring the whole system down, although these are very rare (I have encountered one such issue in four years, and that was my fault). I can't think of the last time I had to force kill a program during normal usage (except cases involving stale NFS mounts, which you probably will not encounter until you know what that means, and what to do about it).

Photo Viewers and Whatnot

Most distros will ship with a full suite of applications required for desktop users, photo viewers included. Common software you will see: * Photo viewer - ex. gwenview, shotwell, feh * Office suite - ex. LibreOffice, OpenOffice * Image editor - ex. Pinta, GIMP * Text editor - ex. GEdit, Mousepad * Web browser - ex. Google Chrome, Firefox * GUI package manager - ex. Synaptic, Octopi, Ubuntu Software Center

Possibly many more, depending on the distro in question. Something like LMDE, you will find, is usually very complete in terms of software that is preinstalled.

Build Compatibility

The described system will work just fine with Linux, but bear in mind that you will probably want to use either the 660M, or the intel HD graphics (usually you can disable on in BIOS). On Windows, Nvidia Optimus switches you between the two as needed based on workload, but Optimus does not work on Linux. You also have the option of using Bumblebee, but that may be beyond your level of technical skill.

Closing Notes

I don't want to be a jerk, but when asking questions of the Linux (or other FOSS) community, try to be a little more clear. At the very least, bullet point your questions. While the v/Linux community tends to be kind, positive, and understanding, many FOSS-related communities would throw a hissy fit over your formatting (for example, us Arch folks are not known for beginner-friendliness, although I try to break that stereotype where possible). I am not trying to be demeaning or anything, but like it or not, formatting and manners will get you a lot further in may circles.
